.WHAT HAS CHANGED...
As of 252 PM EDT Wednesday...

No significant forecast changes.

&&

.KEY MESSAGES...
As of 252 PM EDT Wednesday...

1. Increasingly mild, breezy, and showery weather is expected 
through Friday in advance of a cold front. Sharply drier and 
sunny weather will return on Saturday. 

2. Turning cooler early next week with low chances of showers 
Sunday night into Monday. 

&&

.DISCUSSION...
As of 252 PM EDT Wednesday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: It has been hard to scour out our low cloud deck in 
Vermont, and especially the eastern Champlain Valley, today. Partial 
sunshine has gradually broken out this afternoon with temperatures 
responding in kind, reaching the 70s as of this writing in southern 
St. Lawrence County. The warming trend will be more noticeable with 
our nighttime temperatures as southerly flow and increasing moisture 
helps keep us warmer than normal as we move into October. Looking 
upstream, there are light showers streaming eastward across the 
eastern Great Lakes, so a few sprinkles are possible tonight along 
with plentiful cloud cover. Further modification of our air mass 
will set the stage for unusually warm low temperatures for Friday; 
the EFI highlights the southern and eastern portions of 
Vermont especially, where low temperatures in the low 60s would be 
near/above daily records. (Note sharply cooling temperatures Friday 
night prior to midnight will make records unlikely.)

The latest guidance has backed off on chances of rain for tomorrow 
afternoon, but have maintained some PoPs out of continuity. By and 
large, any appreciable rain will hold off until after sunset. From 
the evening into the early morning hours Friday, showers will only 
slowly sag southeastward such that a good soaking rain looks mainly 
across northern New York from St. Lawrence to Clinton Counties, and 
possibly extending through northwestern Vermont. Friday morning much 
of the steady, and widespread rain, is favored to expand
southeastward through the remainder of northern Vermont and the 
Adirondacks as the system's primary cold front passes through. The 
shorter duration of rain, and plume of anomalous PWAT (REFS mean at 
about 1.8" is near the 99th percentile) dwindling as it pushes 
southeastward, leads to decreasing rainfall amounts during the day. 
Moderate rainfall totals near 1" are most likely in pockets of 
northern New York near US Route 11/western foothills of the 
Adirondacks, and northwestern Vermont due to combination of the 
orientation of the steady rain Friday morning and upslope west-
southwesterly flow. While southerly/southwesterly winds will be
noticeable, especially before rain arrives, the peak of the low
level jet (about 35-40 knots in the 850-925 millibar layer) will
be concurrent with the rain and during the early morning hours.
As such, any impacts look modest and mostly centered around 
recreation and aviation interests with strong stability present.

A secondary cold front is evident in higher resolution model 
guidance for Friday afternoon, and it may have sufficient 
convergence to organize scattered to numerous showers. Given the 
piecemeal nature of this front, unsurprisingly there is limited deep 
moisture by this time so despite ample low level moisture and shear, 
instability will be very shallow and no thunderstorm risk is 
evident. Brief downpours will be possible with these showers, then 
much drier air will begin to make its way to the surface. By 
Saturday morning, dew points will have tumbled from the 60s into the 
40s and skies are very likely to become clear given the deep
northwesterly flow indicated by all guidance in advance of a large 
area of high pressure. Seasonably cool and dry air will make for 
ideal leaf peeping conditions on Saturday.

KEY MESSAGE 2: High pressure slides across the Northeast CONUS and out 
toward the Canadian Maritimes early next week, giving us a dry 
finish to the weekend. A cold front crosses the region Sunday night 
into Monday. The best forcing with this system will remain to our 
north, but still expect scattered showers to be possible with the 
frontal passage. A colder airmass follows the front as high pressure 
returns for mid week. Tuesday looks to be the coldest day with highs 
only in the mid 40s to mid 50s, while overnight lows in the 20s to 
around 30F.

&&

.AVIATION /18Z WEDNESDAY THROUGH MONDAY/...
Through 18Z Thursday...Low clouds/MVFR ceilings have been slow to
lift out of the Champlain Valley and VT, and expect they'll linger
through 21z or so before things improve. VFR under SCT-BKN mid/high
deck expected for the remainder of the TAF period thereafter. Only
exception will be localized IFR/LIFR possible in fog in the favored
valleys in eastern VT, including at MPV. Winds remain light S/SW
this afternoon becoming near calm overnight. They increase again
after 14z Thu, with gusts 15-20 kt possible at BTV/MSS due to
channeling up their respective valleys.

Outlook...

Thursday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance
SHRA.
Friday: Mainly MVFR, with local IFR possible. Likely SHRA.
Friday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Slight chance
SHRA.
Saturday: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Saturday Night: VFR. NO SIG WX.
Sunday: VFR. Slight chance SHRA.
Sunday Night: Mainly VFR, with local MVFR possible. Chance SHRA.
Monday: Mainly VFR, with areas MVFR possible. Slight chance SHRA.

&&
